- Coffee Can filter as codified on Screener: 10-yr consistency of ROCE/ROE > 14–15%, revenue growth > 9–10%, low leverage, plus pledge filter — [Screener: Coffee Can Investing](https://www.screener.in/screens/1125448/coffee-can-investing/)
- Marcellus uses a 3-level check: Level 1 quantitative forensic ratios, Level 2 qualitative accounting/governance checklist (issues not captured by data) — [Elearnmarkets](https://www.elearnmarkets.com/school/units/diamonds-in-the-dust/marcellus-s-3-level-check-to-detect-accounting-frauds)
- SEBI orders show the downside of skipping governance checks even in hyped small caps (Gensol rose on EV/solar narrative before collapse) — [Value Research](https://www.valueresearchonline.com/stories/223978/sebi-bars-gensol-founders-over-ev-loan-diversion-tied-to-blusmart/)

body:
- **Signal chain (the dates are well known but I did not re-source them this session; [UNVERIFIED])**: CUDA launched in 2006–07 (years of "wasted" R&D on GPGPU, criticised by investors at the time). AlexNet in 2012 was trained on two NVIDIA GTX 580 GPUs. Data-center revenue more than doubled in FY17 and FY18 (sourced above). Hyperscaler capex accelerated after ChatGPT (Nov 2022). In May 2023, Q2 FY24 revenue guidance of about $11B against about $7B consensus was the "unmistakable" public signal. The stock then multiplied several times *after* that public signal.
- **Second-order lesson:** the 2016–2018 investor who read data-center growth as an AI "picks and shovels" play was right but suffered a 50%+ drawdown in 2018 when crypto-driven gaming demand collapsed. Mixing the thesis segment (data center) with a cyclical segment (gaming/crypto) creates noisy drawdowns.
- Investors known to have held early include Baillie Gifford (Scottish Mortgage) and Cathie Wood's ARK, which sold much of its position in early 2023 before the run **[UNVERIFIED in this session]**. Selling too early is a recurring failure mode.
- After 2023 the move fits the "earnings engine only" pattern, unlike Radico's "twin engine". Very large earnings beats can produce multibagger returns even as the multiple compresses.
title: multibagger_case_studies › Inferences

body:
- US, CRSP 1926–2016: the majority of common stocks have lifetime buy-and-hold returns below one-month T-bills. About 58% fail to beat T-bills. The top 4% explain the entire net gain of the US market — [Bessembinder, JFE 2018 (ASU PDF)](https://wpcarey.asu.edu/sites/default/files/2021-10/do-stocks-outperform-treasury-bills.pdf); [ASU news](https://news.wpcarey.asu.edu/20180917-do-stocks-outperform-treasury-bills)
- Global, 1990–2020: 63,785 firms in 43 countries. The top 1,526 firms (2.39%) created 100% of net shareholder wealth. The study was funded by Baillie Gifford, and the figures come from a presentation reported by Morningstar — [Morningstar AU](https://www.morningstar.com.au/stocks/only-2-4-of-companies-deliver-all-net-shareholder-wealth)
- Drawdowns: Berkshire, the best performer in Mayer's study, was cut in half at least three times — [TIP](https://www.theinvestorspodcast.com/articles/100-bagger-stocks/). Amazon fell 94% (1999–2001) and took about 10 years to regain its peak — [Motley Fool](https://www.fool.com/investing/2016/06/26/amazon-stocks-history-the-importance-of-patience.aspx). NVIDIA had two 50%+ drawdowns (2018, 2022) — [Yahoo](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/nvidia-down-27-peak-history-100700214.html). Radico fell 74% in 2008 and then went sideways for 8 years — [stockpricearchive](https://stockpricearchive.com/share-price-history-and-returns/radico/)
- Survivorship caveat on Amazon: the many stocks that fell this far and never recovered aren't on anyone's chart — [ChartRow](https://chartrow.com/quote/amzn/drawdown)

body:
`person:group-rajesh-exports` · flag: **poor** · confidence: verified · tickers: RAJESHEXPO

Flag: POOR (pending SEBI case; interim findings, not final). Bengaluru gold refiner/jeweller reporting very large revenues (often Rs 2-3 lakh cr+ consolidated, largely via Swiss refiner Valcambi, bought 2015) at razor-thin margins, with limited segment/geography disclosure and a promoter holding ~54%. Long-standing analyst concerns: revenue quality, cash conversion, related-party trading, and frequent auditor changes; a 2023-24 PLI-linked battery venture (Elest/ACC Energy Storage) whose own auditor later resigned citing regulatory reasons. Regulator action: SEBI appointed BDO India as forensic auditor (Dec-2024); per SEBI's 109-page ex-parte interim order (3-Jun-2026), the forensic auditor was denied access to key records, ERP systems and journal data, and SEBI alleged standalone revenue was overstated by ~Rs 12,557 cr over FY21-FY24 (headlines cite a far larger cumulative 'misrepresentation' figure); promoter Rajesh Mehta was barred from dealing in the company's securities; SEBI ordered a fresh forensic audit and referred statutory auditors' conduct to NFRA (which reportedly opened a probe). The company said it would cooperate and not challenge the interim order, while disputing the allegations. SEBI confirmed its interim directions (Oct-2026). Early signals (visible for years): revenue far out of proportion to assets/employees, non-cooperation with information requests, opaque overseas subsidiary, low dividend relative to reported profits, and turnover-vs-cash-flow gaps. Lesson: when a forensic auditor reports non-cooperation, treat it as a stronger signal than any single number.

- **regulator findings:** SEBI interim Jun-2026 (confirmed Oct-2026): alleged Rs 12,557 cr revenue overstatement; forensic non-cooperation

body:
1. **The avoid leg survives the survivorship check and gets a little stronger.** Lesson L19's rule (treat the bottom
   two SUE quintiles as an avoid/exit flag for ≥ 63 trading days) stands. With the dead firms back in, it is −2.4% vs
   controls per quarter, t ≈ −6, 2018–2025.
2. **The live-only universe was a mild, not a fatal, bias** (≈ 0.35 pp on the avoid leg, ≈ 0.6 pp on T−B, both pointing
   the way v1 §4 predicted). Unlike lesson L28 (pledges), the conclusion does not flip. The reason is the ₹500 cr
   floor: most failures fell below it before they failed.
3. **The cheapest edge is the overlap with distress:** a big earnings miss at a firm that later lands on a distress
   list lost −16.6% vs controls in 13 weeks. That supports pairing the PEAD avoid flag with the stage-2 solvency /
   pledge flags (L27, L28). This is descriptive only (71 events, 16 firms, picked by later fate), not a tested rule.
4. **The long leg is still not proven net of costs** (+1.0%, t 1.7). No change to "don't buy on a positive surprise
   alone."

body:
- **P1 (primary, E, non-financial):** RR(H12, CARD) ≥ **2.0** and firm-cluster CI lower bound > **1.3**.
- **P2 (replication, P):** weighted RR for H12 **or** for O_fail ≥ 1.5 with CI lower bound > 1.0.
- **P1 and P2 → ADOPT** the general cap: any India firm with CARD fired → **minimum (starter) size, no adds**, and
  the balance-sheet question is mandatory, whatever the SUE. The existing stronger rule stays on top: CARD + PEAD
  avoid window → 0 new money. (Minimum size rather than 0 for the general case is fixed now, because a quarter of
  firm-quarters carry the flag and the winner cost is expected to be non-trivial.)
- **P1 only → PROVISIONAL**: same rule but marked provisional, re-test when more data come in.
- **P1 fails → NOT ADOPTED**: keep the cap tied to the PEAD window.
- **Return-cost override:** if flagged firms' 3-year mean excess is *positive* with firm-cluster CI lower bound > 0,
  the cap has a measurable return cost: downgrade an ADOPT to PROVISIONAL and say so.
- **S1/S5 question:** S1 or S5 joins the trigger only if, among CARD = 0 events, its RR(H12) vs CARD = 0 & not-S1/S5
  is ≥ 2.0 with firm-cluster CI lower bound > 1.3 (E). Otherwise they stay "look harder" (L27).
- Winner cost is **reported, not a pass/fail criterion** (asked for). Interpretation fixed now: a cap that blocks a
  share of winners close to the share of all firm-quarters it flags has no selectivity on the upside; the case for it
  rests only on the halving/failure lift.
- Sensitivities (do not decide): all events incl. financials; RED instead of CARD; unknown treated as unflagged;
  live firms only; 2018–21 vs 2022–25; quarter bootstrap.
